name: Biochanin A
lead: Biochanin A is an O-methylated isoflavone, a plant phytoestrogen found in red clover, soy, alfalfa sprouts, peanuts and chickpea.[1] In hair-care marketing, red clover-derived biochanin A is named as a component of Capixyl, a cosmetic peptide-and-isoflavone hair-growth active.

The sources reviewed contain no clinical study of biochanin A for hair. Research on red clover isoflavones concerns other conditions, such as menopausal symptoms and osteopenia, and a 2025 review lists Capixyl among topical hair actives.[2][5]

paras: Wikipedia describes biochanin A as a phytoestrogen and a weak inhibitor of fatty acid amide hydrolase in vitro.[1] A 1998 study examined binding of phytoestrogens to estrogen receptor subtypes.[3] Isoflavone bioavailability in healthy women has been characterised for other isoflavones such as genistein and daidzein.[4]
No studies found on biochanin A for hair. Registered trials of red clover isoflavones address postmenopausal osteopenia, overactive bladder and menopausal symptoms rather than hair.[6][7][8]

card.summary: Red-clover isoflavone named in Capixyl; studied for other things, not hair.

quick.overview:
Biochanin A is a phytoestrogen from red clover and legumes. Hair-care marketing lists it as a component of Capixyl.

No hair-specific human study was found; trials of red clover isoflavones address menopause and bone.
quick.mechanism: It binds estrogen receptors in laboratory assays and weakly inhibits an enzyme in vitro; no hair-growth mechanism is established in the sources reviewed.
quick.risks: As a phytoestrogen it has hormone-receptor activity in lab work; no safety data for topical hair use were found.
